source.title: Pay Attention to MLPs
source.authors: Hanxiao Liu; Zi-Hang Dai; David R. So; Quoc V. Le

record.tranche_reason: The study measures validation MLM perplexity across model sizes and compares architectural variants, providing a conceptual test of scaling with parameter count and of architecture sensitivity. It does not reproduce the original scaling-law fitting procedure.
record.gate_note: The paper explicitly reports that perplexity-parameter relationships for Transformers and gMLPs approximately follow a power law. It also compares pretraining perplexity and downstream task scores across model sizes. The ImageNet results report accuracy, not the held-out language-model loss or a power-law loss relation, so they are not recorded as rows. Values cited from other work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: Its own Table 4 sweep measures MLM validation perplexity against parameter count for Transformers and attention-free gMLPs. The authors state that both follow an approximate power law (Fig. 5). Appendix B varies depth and width at roughly fixed capacity, and Table 4 reports finetuning scores across sizes. The setting is new (MLM, non-attention architecture), so T3 fits better than T2. No exponents are fitted.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that gMLPs match Transformers on MLM pretraining perplexity, which tracks capacity rather than the presence of self-attention. Both families follow approximately power-law perplexity-parameter curves, suggesting Kaplan-style laws apply across families. Finetuning depends on inductive bias as well as perplexity: gMLP is worse on cross-sentence tasks like MNLI. That gap closes with a larger gMLP or a tiny single-head attention, with comparable downstream scaling slopes.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses masked language modeling with BERT-style pretraining on C4 and compares Transformers with gMLPs, rather than reproducing the original autoregressive language-model scaling-law method. It varies depth/model capacity and does not fit the original loss laws or test compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: Perplexity is reported as insensitive to depth at fixed capacity in Appendix B, but worsens beyond 48 layers. Downstream transfer differs by task: gMLPs do better than Transformers on SST-2 in the Section 4.2 sweep and worse on MNLI-m.

fits_no_version.finding: At similar parameter counts, swapping Transformer attention for gMLP gating changes MLM perplexity little (4.26 vs 4.35 at about 110M; 3.47 vs 3.43 at about 360M). Other mechanism choices change it a lot: removing content attention gives 5.64, MLP-Mixer 5.34, linear gMLP 5.14.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pretraining loss at fixed parameter count is largely insensitive to architecture family, provided the token-mixing mechanism is adequate; poor mixing mechanisms cost substantially.

record.problems: The parameter sweep covers a limited range relative to the claim's several orders of magnitude. The paper reports approximate power-law behavior but does not give fitted exponents or test predictions on substantially larger runs. The full-setup results do not establish a power-law fit, and the ablation and depth comparisons alter architecture and sometimes parameter count together.
record.rows_left_out: No rows left out from the reported language-model scaling and architecture comparisons. ImageNet accuracy results were excluded because they do not measure the held-out language-model loss or test a power-law loss relation.

untested.parts: Only parameter count is varied, over about 6x (59–365M) in the controlled sweep, and about 7x for gMLP in Table 6. This is far short of several orders of magnitude. Tokens and compute are not swept for loss, and no exponents are reported.
No fixed-compute allocation of parameters and tokens.
Only depth/width trade-offs in Transformers are tested (Table 10). Heads, FFN ratio and other shape parameters are not varied independently, and parameter counts are not exactly matched.
ImageNet results report accuracy, not a loss scaling law. There are no fine-tuning or repeated-data loss laws.
No variation of fitting method, schedule or parameter counting.

missing.what: Table 6 finetuning scores (SST-2, MNLI m/mm, SQuAD v1.1/v2.0) across base, large and xlarge. Example: the gMLP SQuAD-v2.0 gap shrinks from 8.5 to 2.7 points with scale.
Calibration of finetuning accuracy against pretraining perplexity for Transformer, gMLP and aMLP. Points vary depth (0.5–2x) and data (1–8x).
aMLP scaling curves for perplexity and finetuning in the Section 4.2 setup
Log-perplexity vs log-params plot underlying the authors' power-law statement; no exponents are given

record.verdict_notes: The primary aim is architecture comparison; scaling evidence is a small-range, few-point sweep with no fitted exponents. Table 10 used a 'similar yet different' training setup, and its parameter counts vary from 84M to 110M. MLM perplexity is treated as language-model pretraining loss for V1. ImageNet accuracy vs capacity was correctly excluded from V5.

versions.untested_parts: The study varies parameter count, not training tokens or compute, and does not establish the conditions under which the other quantities are not bottlenecks.
No power-law fit on small runs is used to predict measured losses on runs orders of magnitude larger.
No fixed-compute-budget sweep or loss-minimising parameter/token allocation is tested.
The study tests depth and width changes and several architecture variants, but not a broad, systematic sweep of architecture details at exactly fixed parameter count.
ImageNet classification is evaluated, but the paper does not test whether the same power-law form holds for held-out loss in other modalities or training regimes.
The study evaluates SST-2, MNLI and SQuAD downstream results; it does not establish downstream predictability for other tasks or model families.
The study does not systematically vary parameter-counting conventions, fitting method or training schedule to test the dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocations.
